_meta.translationStatus: English draft awaiting NGO educator sign-off. All people, stipends, prices and amounts are fictional assumptions; no interest is assumed on savings.

hook.1: Kiran: My fictional ₹4,000 stipend just arrived, and there is so much I want to buy!
hook.2: Lata: First tell needs from wants. Needs are must-haves, and wants are good to have and can be postponed.
hook.3: Lata: Let's go home and plan the month before spending anything.

lesson.title: Needs or wants?
lesson.prompt: A need is a must-have. A want is good to have and can be postponed. Kiran is looking at three fictional things. Tap the one that is a need.
lesson.busPassValue: ₹600 for the month, so Kiran can reach school.

decision.title: Plan Kiran's month
decision.prompt: Kiran has ₹4,000 this month. Needs cost ₹2,000 (bus pass, tiffin and school supplies). Share all the money across needs, wants and savings.
decision.hint1: Hint 1: Put the ₹2,000 for needs in first.
decision.hint2: Hint 2: Keep some money for savings, then place what is left in wants.
decision.explanation: Essentials come first, and even a small saving protects you from surprises.

consequence.plan: Kiran's ₹4,000 stipend: needs ₹2,000 are covered first, ₹1,000 goes to wants and ₹1,000 goes to savings.
consequence.savings: Saving ₹1,000 a month, Kiran reaches a ₹6,000 school-trip fund in 6 months. This assumes no interest is added.
consequence.explanation: Kiran paid for needs first, enjoyed some wants and set money aside, so the month balances. If something unexpected comes up, the plan can be revised: move money out of wants before touching needs or savings. All amounts here are fictional.

transfer.explanation: The surprise cost is now part of your needs, so it comes out of what was left. Revise the plan: needs first, some savings, then wants.

rohan.title: Rohan's stipend, with a surprise
rohan.prompt: Rohan has a ₹5,000 stipend. Needs cost ₹2,500. Mid-month, his bicycle chain breaks and the ₹1,000 repair is already added to needs. Revise his plan with all the money placed.
rohan.hint1: Hint 1: Needs are ₹2,500 plus the ₹1,000 repair.
rohan.hint2: Hint 2: Keep some money for savings, then place what is left in wants.

sana.title: Sana's stipend, with a surprise
sana.prompt: Sana has a ₹3,000 stipend. Needs cost ₹1,500. Mid-month, a ₹500 lab fee for a school project comes up and is already added to needs. Revise her plan with all the money placed.
sana.hint1: Hint 1: Needs are ₹1,500 plus the ₹500 fee.
sana.hint2: Hint 2: Keep some money for savings, then place what is left in wants.

no_essentials.review: Your choice: you left too little in needs to cover the essentials. Safer choice: pay for needs first, then keep some savings, then spend on wants. Concept: needs are must-haves, and a budget should prioritise essential expenses. Why it matters: if wants take the money, the bills that matter most go unpaid.

no_savings.review: Your choice: you spent everything and put nothing into savings. Safer choice: after needs are covered, keep a small share of every month for savings. Concept: a budget allocates funds for savings as well as essentials. Why it matters: with no savings, one surprise cost has nothing to be paid from.

want_as_need.review: Your choice: you picked a want as a need. Safer choice: a need is a must-have, like the bus pass Kiran uses to reach school; a concert or café snacks are wants that can wait. Concept: needs are must-haves, whereas wants are good to have and can be postponed. Why it matters: telling them apart first is what lets a budget pay for needs before wants.

claim.needsWants: Needs are must-haves, whereas wants are good to have; wants can be postponed and acquired later.
claim.budget: Budgeting is balancing income and expenses so that expenses are less than income; any surplus can be invested for future needs.
claim.prioritise: A realistic budget tracks income and expenses, allocates funds for savings and prioritises essential expenses.
claim.differentiate: Living below your means involves differentiating between wants and needs.
